title: What artificial intelligence includes
summary: A map of AI before the vocabulary gets in the way: reasoning, learning, perception, generation, and action.
html:
A map of AI before the vocabulary gets in the way: reasoning, learning, perception, generation, and action.

Start with the task

Artificial intelligence studies systems that perform tasks involving perception, reasoning, learning, or decision-making. A system can search a game tree without learning anything. A classifier can learn from labeled examples without generating text. A language model can generate fluent text without checking whether its claims are true. These are different capabilities and need different tests.

The nested families

Machine learning is one approach to AI: fit behavior from data. Deep learning uses layered neural networks to learn representations. Generative models learn to produce samples such as text, images, audio, or molecular structures. An agent combines a policy or model with observations, tools, and an environment in which actions have consequences. These categories overlap; they do not form a leaderboard.

Training and inference

Training changes learned parameters using an objective and data. Inference applies a trained system to new inputs. A prompt usually changes the input context, not the model weights. Retrieval supplies external information. Fine-tuning updates parameters. A production application may use all four and must track which component caused a result.

What to learn first

Understand how computers represent and move data, then the mathematics of vectors, uncertainty, and gradients. Learn a small supervised learning pipeline before studying transformers. After that, choose a branch: build applications, train models, optimize hardware, study multimodal systems, or evaluate risks. Each branch builds on the same shared foundations.

Worked example

ProblemCandidate approachUseful test
Find a routeGraph searchPath cost and constraints
Predict equipment failureSupervised learningRecall at an acceptable false-alarm rate
Answer a policy questionRetrieval plus generationEvidence support and abstention
Control a robotPerception, planning, controlTask success and physical constraint violations

What goes wrong

Treating “AI” as synonymous with a chatbot hides the engineering choices. A deterministic rule can be more suitable than a learned model when the desired behavior is known exactly.

Check your understanding

Does adding a document to an LLM prompt train the model?

Reveal the explanation

No. It conditions this inference request. A training step requires a learning objective and a parameter update.

How the pieces connect

A usable chapter has a flow of decisions, evidence, and checks. Use this diagram as a navigation aid, then test each step on a small real example.

An operating model for what artificial intelligence includes

The first design decision is not “which model?” It is whether the task needs a learned approximation at all. A rule, database query, calculator, optimizer, retrieval system, classifier, and generative model each fail in different ways. The most useful AI systems make those boundaries visible rather than pretending one component can do every job.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Field guide: four decisions in order

1. Frame the task

Frame the task establishes the next constraint. State the input, output, decision, and cost of failure. Begin by making the object of study explicit. A vague input, target, or operating condition creates ambiguity that later computation cannot repair.

Write down the input boundary and the unit of analysis. This makes it possible to distinguish a missing fact from a mismatch between the question and the data or system.

2. Choose a capability

Choose a capability establishes the next constraint. Search, prediction, generation, perception, or control. Now make the mechanism inspectable. Prefer a small run whose intermediate values, examples, or traces can be examined before you automate a larger workflow.

Keep a concrete artifact: a small dataset, a notebook cell, a trace, a benchmark command, or a hand-worked calculation. It is the fastest way to surface hidden assumptions.

3. Test the behavior

Test the behavior establishes the next constraint. Use evidence that matches the intended use. Treat the first result as a measurement, not a conclusion. Compare it with a baseline and vary one assumption at a time so that the observed change has an interpretable cause.

Check a deliberately awkward case alongside the happy path. Boundary conditions, rare examples, and resource limits reveal more than another aggregate score.

4. Operate the system

Operate the system establishes the next constraint. Monitor exceptions, feedback, and changing conditions. Finish by connecting the result to a real choice. Record the operating range, uncertainty, and the condition under which the next person should stop, escalate, or revisit the earlier steps.

Preserve the decision record with the result. A useful technical chapter leaves enough context for a reader to reproduce the reasoning, challenge it, and choose a safe next action.

When the first approach fails

Do not respond to a weak result by immediately adding scale, complexity, or another framework. First locate the failure: the input may not match the intended problem; the representation may discard a useful signal; the measurement may reward the wrong outcome; or the system may have crossed a memory, latency, reliability, or authority boundary. Change one layer, repeat the smallest useful check, and keep the before-and-after evidence.

Gotcha. A polished output can hide an untested assumption. The most convincing demonstration is a counterexample the workflow handles deliberately, with the limitation stated in the release or research record.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Frame the task. State the input, output, decision, and cost of failure.
  2. Choose a capability. Search, prediction, generation, perception, or control.
  3. Test the behavior. Use evidence that matches the intended use.
  4. Operate the system. Monitor exceptions, feedback, and changing conditions.

Write an acceptance test before choosing a model. For each intended action, define the available evidence, an acceptable abstention path, the human or system allowed to act, and what counts as a harmful error.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
